Gender-Based Violence (GBV) and Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) remain significant social and protection concerns that can affect the safety, dignity and wellbeing of individuals and communities. In Kajiado County, barriers such as stigma, fear of retaliation, limited information, concerns about confidentiality and limited access to support services can make reporting and seeking assistance difficult. This project therefore focused on the development of Linda Binti, an AI-powered application designed to support the prevention and response to GBV and FGM through accessible information, confidential reporting, safety guidance and emergency assistance.

The study adopted a descriptive research design to identify user needs and requirements relevant to the development of the application. Primary data were collected using a structured questionnaire, while secondary information was obtained from academic literature, reports, policies and other relevant documented sources. The system was developed using an Agile software development methodology. The implemented solution consists of an Android mobile application developed using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, a
-based backend, a pilot-scale SQLite database and a browser-based dashboard developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet for geographical

. The application incorporates confidential reporting, educational information, risk assessment, Safety Compass, trusted emergency contacts, GSM-based SOS messaging, survivor support and a hybrid AI assistant. The AI assistant combines offline rules and knowledge with optional cloud-based AI functionality, with fallback to offline assistance when the cloud service is unavailable.

The developed system was tested to verify the functionality of its major components. A total of 255 application tests and 140 backend tests were conducted, with no failures recorded. The system was developed within the defined project scope for Kajiado County and is intended to complement, rather than replace, existing emergency, health, government and support services. The completed application demonstrates how mobile technology, privacy-aware design, location functionality and
AI-assisted information can be integrated to provide accessible digital support for GBV and FGM prevention and response.

Existing literature indicates that GBV and FGM are complex social and public health concerns that cannot be adequately explained through individual

alone. They are influenced by interactions among gender relations, family expectations, community norms, cultural beliefs, economic conditions, access to services, legislation and institutional responses (WHO, 2021, 2025; UNICEF, 2020). Although GBV and FGM are distinct forms of harm, the literature identifies several interconnected mechanisms, including unequal gender relations, social expectations, pressure to conform, stigma, fear of rejection and limited access to appropriate support (Grose et al., 2019; Mwendwa et al., 2022; WHO, 2025). This section therefore reviews evidence across different contexts before focusing on Kenya and Kajiado County and examining how digital technologies can contribute to prevention and response.

Female genital mutilation refers to procedures involving partial or total removal of the external female genitalia or other injury to female genital organs for non-medical reasons (WHO, 2025). The WHO estimates that more than 230 million girls and women alive today have undergone FGM in countries where population-level data are available, with the majority of procedures performed on girls before the age of 15 (WHO, 2025). FGM has no health benefits and may result in immediate and long-term physical, psychological, sexual and reproductive health complications (WHO, 2025).

The persistence of FGM demonstrates why the practice needs to be examined as a social and cultural issue in addition to a health issue. WHO (2025) explains that reasons for FGM vary between communities but may include social conventions, pressure to conform, the desire for social acceptance, fear of rejection, preparation for adulthood or marriage, and beliefs concerning female sexuality. The practice can therefore continue even where individuals may be aware of its harmful consequences because social expectations can influence family decision-making.

The concept of social conformity is particularly important. Where FGM operates as a social norm, parents may believe that failing to have a daughter undergo the practice could result in social rejection, reduced marriage prospects or negative judgement from other community members

(WHO, 2025). In such circumstances, the decision is not necessarily based on a single person’s preference. Instead, it may reflect expectations about what other families are doing or what the community considers acceptable.

Somalia provides an important international example. UNICEF (2022) reported that FGM was deeply embedded in social and cultural practices and that some families associated the practice with chastity, marriageability and social acceptance. Religious misconceptions have also contributed to the continuation of FGM in some communities, although WHO (2025) notes that no religious scripts prescribe the practice. This distinction is important because religious belief and cultural practice should not automatically be treated as the same phenomenon.

The Somali experience further illustrates the intergenerational nature of social norms. When parents believe that an uncut girl may experience social exclusion or difficulty marrying, they may perceive FGM as a protective or socially necessary practice even when it carries known health risks. Such perceptions can allow the practice to continue from one generation to another (UNICEF, 2022; WHO, 2025).

Kenya has made considerable progress in reducing FGM. The KDHS 2022 reported that 15% of women aged 15–49 had undergone FGM, compared with 38% in 1998 (KNBS & ICF, 2023). The same survey found that most women and men who had heard of FGM did not believe that religion required the practice, and more than nine in ten believed that the practice should not continue (KNBS & ICF, 2023). These findings demonstrate an important decline in acceptance at national level while also showing that attitudes and practices do not always change at the same rate.

The persistence of FGM despite increasing opposition illustrates the importance of community-level norms. Grose et al. (2019), using nationally representative Kenyan data, examined community influences on FGM/C and demonstrated the importance of contextual factors, norms and ethnic diversity in understanding the persistence of the practice. Their findings support the argument that interventions should not focus exclusively on individual knowledge but should also consider the social environment in which decisions concerning girls are made.

Linda Binti incorporated FGM education, prevention information, safety guidance and support-oriented content in response to these findings. The purpose was to provide accessible information that could help users understand the health and social dimensions of FGM and identify appropriate
prevention or support options. The application therefore treated FGM as a multidimensional issue rather than simply as a medical condition.

2.2.4 GBV and FGM in Kenya and Kajiado County

Kenya has developed legal and policy frameworks addressing GBV and FGM. The Prohibition of Female Genital Mutilation Act, 2011 established legal prohibitions against FGM, while the Protection Against Domestic Violence Act, 2015 established a framework for protection from domestic violence (Republic of Kenya, 2011, 2015). These measures demonstrate national recognition that GBV and FGM require formal legal and institutional responses.

However, legal frameworks do not eliminate all social and practical barriers. The KDHS 2022 provides evidence that GBV and FGM remain relevant public health and social concerns in Kenya despite the country’s legal and policy measures (KNBS & ICF, 2023). The survey reported that 15% of women aged 15–49 had undergone FGM, while 34% had experienced physical violence since age 15 (KNBS & ICF, 2023). These figures indicate that legal prohibition and declining prevalence have occurred alongside continued exposure to violence and harmful practices.

The KDHS also demonstrates the importance of examining local contexts. KNBS provides county-specific fact sheets, including a fact sheet for Kajiado County, allowing national findings to be considered alongside county-level conditions (KNBS, 2023). This supports the argument that national averages may conceal substantial differences in prevalence, attitudes, service access and social conditions between counties.

2.2.5 Existing Digital Solutions for GBV and FGM Prevention and Response

Digital technologies have increasingly been considered as tools for supporting GBV prevention and response. Mobile applications can provide information, emergency communication, reporting mechanisms, safety planning and access to support resources. However, the effectiveness of a digital intervention depends on its usability, safety, privacy, accessibility and suitability for the population for which it is developed (Eisenhut et al., 2020).

Eisenhut et al. (2020) conducted a systematic review of mobile applications addressing violence against women. Out of 327 relevant applications identified, 171 were included in the review and classified into five main functional categories: emergency, avoidance, education, reporting and evidence building, and supporting applications. Emergency applications represented the largest

category, accounting for 46.78% of the reviewed applications, followed by education at 21.05%, reporting and evidence building at 14.04%, supporting applications at 12.28% and avoidance applications at 5.85%.

The findings reveal an important limitation in existing digital approaches. A large proportion of applications focused primarily on immediate emergency or avoidance functions, while fewer applications combined multiple functions (Eisenhut et al., 2020). This is significant because GBV and FGM prevention and response involve multiple needs. A person may require education before violence occurs, safety guidance during a risk situation, reporting support after an incident and referral information when seeking longer-term assistance.

The systematic review also highlighted the importance of data security, personal safety and efficacy when evaluating mobile interventions (Eisenhut et al., 2020). This is particularly relevant to GBV and FGM because information about survivors, locations, reports and trusted contacts can be highly sensitive. A poorly designed application could create additional risks if another person discovers the application, accesses stored information or obtains sensitive location data.

2.2.6 Artificial Intelligence in GBV and FGM Support

Artificial intelligence has become increasingly relevant to digital health and information systems because it can support information retrieval, conversational interfaces, classification and decision-support functions. However, the use of AI in sensitive areas requires careful consideration of accuracy, privacy, human oversight, transparency, fairness and safety (WHO, 2021).

The WHO (2021) guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health identifies human autonomy, safety, public interest, transparency, explainability, privacy, equity and accountability as important principles. These principles are particularly relevant when AI systems interact with people experiencing GBV or seeking information about FGM because users may make important decisions based on the information presented.

AI should therefore be treated as a support mechanism rather than an unquestionable authority. An AI system may provide general information but may not understand all contextual factors in a user’s situation. It may also produce inaccurate or incomplete information. For this reason, AI-based support should not replace qualified healthcare workers, counsellors, police officers, lawyers or other professionals.

Linda Binti incorporated a hybrid AI approach consistent with these considerations. The reviewed literature demonstrates substantial international and Kenyan research on GBV, FGM, social norms and digital interventions, but several gaps remain. First, international evidence demonstrates that GBV and FGM are influenced by context-specific social and cultural factors. Research in Bangladesh has linked men’s violence against women to gender norms, beliefs, masculinity and power relations (Fattah & Camellia, 2020), while evidence from Somalia has demonstrated the importance of community norms in both GBV prevention and survivor support (UNICEF, 2020, 2021). Research on FGM has similarly demonstrated the importance of social acceptance, conformity, marriage expectations and fear of rejection (WHO, 2025). These findings demonstrate that interventions cannot simply be transferred from one country or community to another without considering local circumstances.

Second, Kenyan evidence demonstrates that community-level attitudes and contextual factors influence FGM. Grose et al. (2019) found that community influences were important in understanding FGM/C in Kenya, while Mwendwa et al. (2022) specifically identified culture, men’s roles, knowledge and

education as important themes in Kajiado and Meru. However, this literature also indicates the need for approaches that combine knowledge, community engagement and practical support rather than relying on a single intervention mechanism.

Third, the review of digital interventions identified a functional gap. Eisenhut et al. (2020) found that emergency applications constituted the largest category of mobile applications addressing violence against women, while fewer applications combined multiple functions. The authors also

highlighted the need for further attention to data security, personal safety and effectiveness. This suggests a need for digital systems that integrate prevention and response while maintaining appropriate privacy safeguards.

Fourth, many digital systems depend on network connectivity. For users in contexts where internet access may be inconsistent, an application that relies entirely on cloud services may become inaccessible when support is most needed. The literature therefore supports consideration of offline functionality alongside optional online services.

Fifth, there is a need to balance technological innovation with safety. AI, GPS, SMS and web dashboards can increase functionality, but each introduces privacy, accuracy, security or misuse considerations (Eisenhut et al., 2020; WHO, 2021). A digital system for GBV and FGM must therefore be designed around the safety and autonomy of its users rather than around technology alone.
The identified gaps informed the development of Linda Binti as a locally

, multifunctional application for GBV and FGM prevention and response in Kajiado County. The developed system integrated educational information, reporting support, safety guidance, emergency communication, trusted contacts, optional location sharing, hybrid AI support and an

web dashboard. It incorporated offline functionality and privacy-oriented features while maintaining the position that digital support should complement, rather than replace, professional healthcare, counselling, police, legal and community services. The research gap therefore concerned not the complete absence of digital GBV or FGM interventions, but the need for an integrated, context-sensitive and privacy-conscious system that brings several relevant functions together within the Kajiado context.

Secondary data were obtained from academic literature and other relevant documented sources reviewed during the literature review in Chapter Two. Secondary sources provide existing knowledge and evidence that can be used to establish the background of a research problem, identify existing approaches and support interpretation of primary findings (Saunders et al., 2023).

The secondary sources used in the study included academic journal articles, previous studies, reports, policies and other relevant publications concerning GBV, FGM, digital technology, artificial intelligence, mobile applications, emergency support, privacy and technology-based interventions. Reviewing existing literature enabled the researcher to understand what was already known about the research problem and identify areas requiring further technological consideration (Creswell & Creswell, 2022).

The literature reviewed in Chapter Two was also used to understand the social and cultural factors associated with GBV and FGM. Particular attention was given to issues such as social norms, stigma, family expectations, fear of rejection, reporting barriers, access to assistance and the role of technology in supporting prevention and response. This contextual information was important because a technological solution must address the circumstances in which users may require support rather than focusing only on the technical functionality of the application.

Secondary data also provided information about existing digital approaches for supporting individuals affected by GBV and FGM. The review of existing digital solutions enabled the researcher to examine common features, identify limitations and establish areas where Linda Binti could provide an integrated approach. The literature review in Chapter Two showed that digital interventions may support areas such as information provision, emergency communication, reporting, location-based assistance and digital monitoring, but that privacy, safety, accessibility and contextual suitability must be considered when designing such systems.

The secondary information was compared with the primary findings obtained from the questionnaire. This comparison helped identify areas of agreement and issues that required consideration during the development of Linda Binti. Comparing information from different sources can strengthen the interpretation of research findings by allowing primary evidence to be examined alongside established knowledge (Saunders et al., 2023).

The secondary data also supported the selection and justification of technological features implemented in Linda Binti. The findings concerning digital access and connectivity supported consideration of offline functionality. Evidence concerning confidentiality and the sensitive nature of GBV and FGM supported the inclusion of privacy and access-control mechanisms. Literature concerning emergency communication supported the inclusion of trusted contacts, emergency assistance and optional location sharing. The findings concerning AI and digital support informed the use of a hybrid AI approach in which offline knowledge and rules remain available while optional cloud-based AI assistance can be used when the required conditions are met.

The information obtained from secondary sources therefore complemented the primary data collected through the questionnaire. While primary data provided direct information from selected respondents, secondary data provided the academic, contextual and technological foundation needed to interpret those responses and establish appropriate system requirements. Together, the two sources supported the requirements analysis that guided the design and development activities described in Chapter Three.

The results indicate that the implemented automated test suites completed without recorded failures. The mobile tests covered the application’s core local functionality and supporting components, while the backend tests covered the server-side implementation and its services. The result provided evidence that the implemented software components were functioning as expected under the tested conditions.

The results should, however, be interpreted within the scope of the tests performed. A zero-failure result does not mean that every possible real-world condition or security vulnerability has been eliminated. In particular, the delivered project was a prototype/pilot-scale system and was not subjected to a county-wide operational deployment or a full independent penetration test.

The system was evaluated against the requirements identified during the requirement-gathering and analysis stages. Particular attention was given to privacy, confidentiality, offline availability, emergency assistance, local reporting, language support and access to information.

The implemented application addressed these requirements through an offline-first design. Users could access core educational information, perform risk assessment, maintain trusted contacts and create reports locally without requiring continuous internet connectivity. The application also incorporated English, Kiswahili and Maa support in the implemented content.

The requirement for emergency assistance was addressed through trusted-contact SOS messaging, optional location sharing and access to established emergency numbers. The requirement for confidential reporting was addressed through local-first report storage, consent-controlled

The application also provided educational information, safety guidance, survivor support information and an AI-assisted interface. The AI functionality was implemented as a support feature and was not designed to replace professional counselling, medical services, legal services or emergency responders.

The questionnaire results from the requirement-gathering stage were intended to provide further user-level validation of the identified needs. Where final questionnaire statistics or user-acceptance scores were not available, no numerical usability score was assigned. Focus-group testing was not reported in the project evidence, so no focus-group findings are presented. The questionnaire in Chapter Four was used to gather requirements. It is not treated here as a scored post-implementation test. This avoided presenting unverified evaluation results as completed findings.

Although the system underwent functional, integration and security-oriented testing, several limitations remained. First, the application was developed and evaluated as a pilot-scale system rather than through a county-wide operational deployment. Therefore, the testing did not establish performance under the full volume of users that could potentially access such a service across Kajiado County.

Second, the system’s SOS functionality depends on the availability of the device’s GSM service, appropriate permissions, configured trusted contacts and, where required, a location fix. Testing therefore could not guarantee successful delivery under every possible network or device condition.

Third, the optional cloud AI functionality depends on backend configuration, network availability, user consent and an available AI service key. The application includes offline and rules-based fallback mechanisms, but the testing did not represent a guarantee of continuous external AI availability.
Fourth, the USSD component was implemented as a gateway-ready service and demonstration pathway rather than as a live public
. Consequently, the testing did not represent live operator-level USSD performance.

Finally, although security controls were tested within the project scope, the system was not subjected to a full independent penetration test or formal security certification. Security testing therefore provides evidence of the implemented controls but should not be interpreted as proof that all possible vulnerabilities have been eliminated.

The discussion is limited to the findings and implementation already presented in this report. The requirement-gathering questionnaire and the literature review identified barriers to reporting, the need for confidentiality, and the value of accessible information on GBV and FGM in Kajiado County. The implemented system responds to those requirements through a discreet Android application, local reporting, education, risk assessment, the Safety Compass, trusted-contact SOS by GSM SMS, survivor support information and an optional hybrid AI assistant.

Chapter Six showed that the system was built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose on Android, Room for local SQLite storage, and a Ktor backend with its own SQLite database. The NGO dashboard uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Leaflet. It does not use Flutter, Firebase or Google Maps for the dashboard. Emergency calls to 999, 112, 1195 and 116 open the phone dialler. The application does not dispatch the police and does not replace counselling, healthcare or legal services.

The testing reported in this chapter recorded 255 mobile tests and 140 backend tests, with no recorded failures in those suites. That result applies only to the tests that were run. Section 7.9 already states that the system was a pilot-scale prototype, that SOS delivery depends on the device and the mobile network, that online AI depends on configuration and consent, and that USSD was gateway-ready rather than a live public shortcode. The discussion therefore does not treat the zero-failure result as evidence of county-wide deployment or of a completed security certification.
The recommendations below follow from the limitations already stated in Sections 1.6 and 7.9 and from the functions that were actually implemented.

1. Any later use beyond this prototype should remain within Kajiado County and should be arranged with the relevant health, community and NGO partners. The present project did not deploy the system county-wide.
2. A live USSD service should be introduced only after a licensed gateway and an operator shortcode are in place. The current menu should continue to be described as gateway-ready.
3. The Somali language option should not be described as complete until a full content pack is added. English, Kiswahili and Maa are the implemented content languages.

4. An independent security review would be appropriate before any wider operational use. The project tested the implemented controls, but it did not include a full penetration test or a security certification.
5. Linda Binti should continue to complement 999, 112, 1195 and 116, and it should not be presented as a replacement for police, clinical, legal or counselling services.

The study set out to investigate challenges affecting the reporting of and response to GBV and FGM in Kajiado County, to examine existing digital approaches, to develop Linda Binti, and to test the developed system. The literature review and the requirement-gathering questionnaire addressed the first two objectives within the limits of the sources and respondents used. The third objective was met by the Android application and Ktor backend described in Chapter Six, including offline-first local functions, GSM SMS to trusted contacts, hybrid AI support and the NGO dashboard.

The fourth objective was addressed through the functional, backend, integration and security checks in this chapter. The recorded automated suites contained 395 tests and no recorded failures. Those results support the claim that the tested functions behaved as implemented. They do not support a claim of live county-wide operation, live public USSD, automatic police integration, or a substitute for professional response services. Within that scope, Linda Binti provides a discreet, locally contextualised prototype for GBV and FGM prevention and response in Kajiado County.
